issues.legal_issue: A civil court cannot decide a disputed sub-tenancy’s lawfulness when the rent authority is empowered to decide that issue during the period in which the civil suit is filed.
material_facts: The claimants occupied the accommodation as sub-tenants and sought a declaration that they had become direct tenants because the sub-tenancy was lawful.
The landlord disputed that the sub-tenancy was lawful.
The claimants filed their suit within the period in which an application to the Rent Controlling Authority could be made to decide the dispute.
issues.conclusion: The civil court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the suit because the Rent Controlling Authority was empowered to decide the disputed lawfulness of the sub-tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 15(2) and 15(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, the Rent Controlling Authority could decide a contested dispute about the lawfulness of a pre-existing sub-tenancy on a timely application. Section 16(2) made lawful subletting necessary for a sub-tenant to become a direct tenant. Section 45(1) barred a civil court from entertaining a suit concerning a matter the Authority was empowered to decide. No earlier cases were relied upon.

predicates.landlord_contests_subletting_lawfulness: The landlord disputed that the premises had been lawfully sublet to the claimants.
predicates.suit_filed_within_authority_decision_per: The sub-tenants filed their suit while the period for seeking the rent authority’s decision on the subletting dispute remained open.

issues.definition: When sub-tenants seek direct tenancy in a civil suit, the landlord disputes the lawfulness of the subletting, and the suit is filed while the rent authority can decide that dispute, the civil court lacks jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A prior ejectment decree against the tenant does not remove the rent authority’s power to decide a timely dispute about the lawfulness of the sub-tenancy or make a civil court competent to decide it.
material_facts: The landlord had obtained an ejectment decree against the tenant before the sub-tenants filed their suit.
The sub-tenants’ suit was filed within the period for applying to the Rent Controlling Authority to decide whether the subletting was lawful.
The sub-tenants claimed that lawful subletting gave them direct tenancy rights despite the decree.
issues.conclusion: The ejectment decree did not make the civil court competent to decide the dispute; the Rent Controlling Authority remained empowered to decide it during the applicable period.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15(3) and 45(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, applied to the timely dispute over lawful subletting even though the landlord had already obtained an ejectment decree against the tenant. No earlier cases were relied upon.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s failure to seek a determination of the subletting dispute does not establish that the subletting was lawful or relieve the sub-tenant claiming direct tenancy of proving it.
material_facts: The claimants sought direct tenancy on the basis that the premises had been lawfully sublet to them.
The landlord had not applied to the Rent Controlling Authority to determine whether the subletting was lawful.
The claimants’ suit was filed before the period for such an application had expired.
issues.conclusion: The claimants had to establish that the subletting was lawful; the landlord’s failure to apply did not establish lawfulness or direct tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, required lawful subletting for a sub-tenant to become a direct tenant. The party claiming that right had to establish the required lawful subletting; the landlord’s failure to seek a determination under section 15(3) did not satisfy that burden. No earlier cases were relied upon.

issues.definition: When a sub-tenant claims direct tenancy and the landlord did not seek a determination of the subletting dispute, the sub-tenant must still prove lawful subletting.

issues.legal_issue: The civil-court exception for property-title questions does not confer jurisdiction to decide whether a sub-tenancy was lawful for purposes of a statutory direct-tenancy claim.
material_facts: The claimants relied on a statutory right to be treated as direct tenants because the accommodation had been lawfully sublet to them.
Their claim required a decision on the lawfulness of the subletting.
They invoked the civil-court exception for questions of title to accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The title exception did not authorize the civil court to decide the lawfulness of the subletting or make it competent to entertain the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 45(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, preserved civil-court jurisdiction over questions of title or interests in property existing apart from the Act, including matters incidentally addressed by the rent authority. It did not extend to a statutory right to direct tenancy under section 16(2) or to the lawfulness of subletting that had to be decided under section 15(3). No earlier cases were relied upon.
